subject: paediatrics
title: Pediatric Spinal Dysraphism and Acute Meningitis: CSF Analysis

steps.tx: Failure of dorsal neural tube closure during the fourth week of embryogenesis generates severe spinal dysraphism. The most complex viable variant is **lumbar meningomyelocele in infants**, in which both the meninges and the dysplastic spinal neural placode protrude through a posterior vertebral arch defect. Affected infants demonstrate flaccid lower extremity paraparesis, absent deep tendon reflexes, bilateral talipes equinovarus, sensory denervation, and neurogenic bladder.
steps.say: Meningomyelocele involves herniation of the meninges and spinal cord placode through a vertebral arch defect. Infants have lower limb paralysis, clubfoot, and neurogenic bladder.

left.title: Meningomyelocele Features
points: Sac contains meninges, CSF, and neural placode
Flaccid lower limb paraparesis and sensory loss
Continuous dribbling from neurogenic bladder
Almost 100% associated with Chiari II malformation

right.title: Immediate Neonatal Management
points: Place infant prone with hips slightly flexed
Cover defect with warm sterile saline-soaked gauze
Administer broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics
Perform surgical closure within 48 hours of birth

steps.tx: Herniation of the cerebellar vermis and brainstem through the foramen magnum accompanies virtually all open spinal lesions. The classic **Arnold-Chiari Type II malformation** leads to downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils, elongation of the fourth ventricle, and obstructive aqueductal stenosis, precipitating progressive hydrocephalus in over eighty percent of children with meningomyelocele, frequently requiring ventriculoperitoneal shunt insertion.
steps.say: Chiari II malformation accompanies almost all cases of myelomeningocele. Hindbrain herniation obstructs cerebrospinal fluid pathways, precipitating severe progressive hydrocephalus.

rows: Downward tonsillar herniation through foramen magnum
Compression of caudal cranial nerve nuclei (IX-XII)
Loss of motor power, progressive scoliosis
Surgical detethering of the spinal cord

steps.tx: Hematogenous seeding of the subarachnoid space triggers severe leptomeningeal inflammation and parenchymal edema. In infants beyond the neonatal period, **pediatric acute bacterial meningitis** is predominantly caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis, whereas group B Streptococcus and Escherichia coli predominate in neonates. Young infants present with fever, paradoxical irritability where crying worsens when held, a bulging fontanelle, and high-pitched neurological crying.
steps.say: Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis are the commonest causes of bacterial meningitis beyond the neonatal period. Paradoxical irritability and a bulging fontanelle are key signs.

vis.alt: Clinical illustration depicting classic signs of pediatric meningitis including neck stiffness, Kernig sign, and purpuric rash.
vis.caption: Meningeal irritation signs, bulging fontanelle, and purpuric vasculitic rash in acute bacterial meningitis. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Physical examination in older children demonstrates classical signs of meningeal irritation elicited by stretching inflamed spinal roots. The hallmark signs are **nuchal rigidity and Brudzinski sign**, where passive flexion of the child's neck induces involuntary flexion of the hips and knees. Kernig sign is demonstrated by inability to comfortably extend the knee beyond one hundred and thirty-five degrees when the hip is flexed at ninety degrees.
steps.say: Nuchal rigidity, Kernig sign, and Brudzinski sign reflect inflammation of the spinal meninges. Neck flexion triggering hip flexion represents a positive Brudzinski sign.

left.title: Meningeal Irritation Signs
points: Nuchal rigidity: involuntary resistance to passive neck flexion
Brudzinski sign: passive neck flexion flexes hips and knees
Kernig sign: resistance to knee extension with hip at 90 degrees
Tripod sign: child sits leaning back supporting on hands

right.title: Atypical Neonatal Signs
points: Meningeal signs characteristically absent under 1 year
Hypothermia, poor feeding, apnea, lethargy
Full, bulging, tense anterior fontanelle
High-pitched cerebral cry and seizures

steps.tx: Lumbar puncture and urgent cerebrospinal fluid examination provide definitive diagnostic confirmation in suspected central nervous system infections. Characteristic **cerebrospinal fluid findings in bacterial meningitis** include a cloudy or turbid appearance, marked pleocytosis with thousands of polymorphonuclear neutrophils, markedly elevated protein concentration exceeding one hundred milligrams per decilitre, and profoundly depressed CSF glucose below forty percent of simultaneous blood glucose.
steps.say: Cerebrospinal fluid in bacterial meningitis shows neutrophil pleocytosis, high protein over one hundred, and low glucose under forty percent of blood glucose.

vis.alt: Differential diagnostic table and collection tubes demonstrating CSF characteristics in bacterial, viral, and tuberculous meningitis.
vis.caption: Cerebrospinal fluid characteristics distinguishing acute bacterial, viral, and tuberculous central nervous system infections. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Comparative cerebrospinal fluid profiles distinguish acute bacterial from aseptic viral and fungal meningitides accurately. In **pediatric aseptic viral meningitis**, the fluid is clear with modest lymphocytic pleocytosis rarely exceeding five hundred cells, normal or minimally elevated protein below eighty milligrams, and normal glucose concentration, whereas tuberculous meningitis exhibits a cobweb coagulum, lymphocyte predominance, very high protein, and markedly depressed glucose.
steps.say: Viral meningitis yields clear CSF with lymphocyte predominance and normal glucose. Tuberculous meningitis demonstrates low glucose, very high protein, and a cobweb coagulum.

steps.tx: Immediate empiric antimicrobial therapy must never be delayed for neuroimaging or diagnostic lumbar puncture. First-line therapy for **empiric bacterial meningitis treatment** in infants older than three months comprises intravenous ceftriaxone (one hundred milligrams per kilogram daily) or cefotaxime, combined with intravenous vancomycin to cover penicillin-resistant pneumococci. In neonates under three months, intravenous ampicillin is added to ensure coverage against Listeria monocytogenes.
steps.say: Start intravenous ceftriaxone and vancomycin immediately for bacterial meningitis. In neonates, add ampicillin to cover Listeria monocytogenes.

left.title: Empiric Antibiotic Regimens
points: Neonates (<3 months): Ampicillin + Cefotaxime
Infants & Children: Ceftriaxone + Vancomycin
High therapeutic doses to cross blood-brain barrier
Duration: 7 to 10 days for meningococcus, 14 for pneumococcus

right.title: Adjunctive Dexamethasone Protocol
points: Give 0.15 mg/kg IV immediately before or with first antibiotic
Continue every 6 hours for 2 to 4 days in H. influenzae / pneumococcus
Significantly reduces sensorineural hearing loss
Has no benefit if administered after antibiotics

steps.tx: Severe purpuric skin manifestations accompany life-threatening meningococcal septicemia and adrenal hemorrhage. Massive endotoxemia induces profound disseminated intravascular coagulation, resulting in **Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome**, characterized by bilateral adrenal hemorrhagic necrosis, refractory septic shock, and widespread petechial and purpuric cutaneous ecchymoses. Management requires aggressive fluid resuscitation, inotropic support, and stress-dose intravenous hydrocortisone.
steps.say: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome causes bilateral adrenal hemorrhage, purpura fulminans, and refractory shock during meningococcemia. Administer stress-dose hydrocortisone immediately.

rows: Exudation of fluid across inflamed arachnoid
Persistent fever, focal seizures, fontanelle fullness
Serial ultrasound; aspirate only if symptomatic
Fibrotic obliteration of arachnoid basilar cisterns
